newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU rallies against U.S. sanction on Cuba.
newsitem.headline: EU rallies against U.S. sanction on Cuba.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers, withholding support for U.S. attacks on Iraq, delivered a second snub to Washington on Sunday, reiterating their sharp criticism of U.S. trade laws against Cuba, Iran and Libya.

"We are entirely of one view in the European Union that any attempt at extra-territoriality is unacceptable," British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind told reporters. "The issue is clear and unanimous and causes now problems."

The ministers, in a second day of informal talks in the southern Irish town of Tralee, discussed the U.S. D'Amato and Helms-Burton laws, designed to punish Iran and Libya for alleged support for terrorism and Cuba for its failure to democratise under Fidel Castro.

Washington's European trading partners have been infuriated by the so-called extra-territoriality in the laws, under European companies could be subject to sanctions for conducting certain types of business with the three countries.
The European Commission, the EU's executive, has been drafting retaliatory measures on instructions from the foreign ministers.
"We all agree that it would be helpful for the EU to develop a policy we can all endorse," Rifkind said.
But in a move to meet some of Washington's concerns, Rifkind said there was string support for the aims of the U.S. laws, if not the means.
The EU has threatened to take the Cuba law to the World Trade Organisation. Rifkind said no decision had been taken, but that it was "quite possible" that such a move would be forthcoming.
Sunday's talks follow the failure of the ministers on their first day of discussions to give Washington backing for its attacks on Iraq to punish Saddam Hussein for an incursion into Kurdish areas.
EU ministers called on Iraq to withdraw from "safe havens" set up for Kurds after the 1991 Gulf War and said they backed the territorial integrity and sovereignty of all states in the region.
France had voiced reservations about Clinton's Iraqi raids, in stark contrast to the wholehearted support Washington received from Britain.
The EU said it wanted an oil-for-food deal with Iraq to go ahead as soon as United Nations Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali deemed that the situation on the ground merited it.
The deal would allow Iraq to sell a limited amount of oil, despite international trade sanctions, to buy badly needed food and medicine.

Following a briefing by international Bosnia mediator Carl Bildt, the EU ministers also agreed to a two-year peace transition period for Bosnia, a move diplomats said indicated the EU's intention to stay engaged in the region following September 14 elections.
Bildt said on Sunday that there was wide agreement among the EU ministers that new elections in Bosnia should be held in September 1998.
Other items to be discussed on Sunday included the status of the bloc's treaty talks, the so-called inter-governmental conference (IGC)

Officials said the ministers would be given a report by the group negotiating the treaty. Ireland would also formally call a special EU summit for October 5 to discuss the IGC and other pending EU business.
IGC negotiators have been instructed to present a draft treaty to a second EU summit in Dublin in December.
